questions.explanation: On the second try the narrator turned too early and stopped a full metre from the curb. Bumping the curb was the first try, and stopping in the road was the third.
options: The back tire bumped the curb.
The car stopped too far from the curb.
The car stopped in the middle of the road.
The car touched the blue van.

questions.stem: The front of the car stuck out "like a dog's tongue." This comparison suggests the car was
questions.explanation: A dog's tongue hangs out to one side, so the car's front was sticking out into the road at an angle. The comparison is about position, not speed or sound.
options: moving fast and out of control
parked neatly along the curb
poking awkwardly into the road
making a loud panting noise

questions.stem: Why was Dad's little "hmm" noise "worse" than words?
questions.explanation: Dad said nothing after the second mistake, and his quiet "hmm" left the narrator to imagine what he thought. He was not shouting, and the man with groceries arrives later.
options: Dad was shouting at the narrator.
It scared the man with groceries.
It meant Dad would take the wheel.
It felt like quiet disappointment.

questions.stem: What does Dad mean by "You can't do it yet. That's a different sentence"?
questions.explanation: Adding "yet" turns a dead end into something still being learned. Dad then teaches a method, so he is not taking over or changing streets.
options: Not managing something now doesn't mean never managing it.
The narrator should say things to Dad more politely.
The narrator should practise on a different street.
Dad will park the car himself this time.

questions.stem: What finally helps the narrator park the car successfully?
questions.explanation: Dad shows the narrator to start turning when the mirror lines up with the van's back bumper, and the next try works. Turning too early had caused the second mistake.
options: Waiting until the street was completely empty
Using the van's bumper as a mark for turning
Turning the wheel as early as possible
Asking the man with groceries for help

questions.stem: Dad's words "Ten more times. Then it's yours" suggest he believes
questions.explanation: Dad wants the narrator to repeat the method until it is reliable, so "it's yours" means the skill, not the parking space. He is grinning, not doubting the narrator.
options: the narrator got lucky and will fail next time
the narrator should stop for the day
practice will turn one success into a skill
the parking space belongs to the family

questions.stem: What two things did the narrator promise during the campaign? Choose two.
questions.explanation: The narrator promised a quiet study room open at lunch and a better lost-and-found system. March is when the study room was finished, not a dance.
options: A better system for the lost and found
Longer lunch breaks
A quiet study room open at lunch
A school dance in March
New lockers for every student

questions.stem: When the narrator says "It's fine" about thirty times, the reader can tell the narrator
questions.explanation: The next sentence, "It was not fine," shows the narrator was covering up how much losing hurt. The narrator smiles at the others rather than showing anger.
options: is hiding disappointment
is glad the election is over
does not care about the result
is angry at the other students

questions.stem: When Noor says "That's not what I asked," what is she pointing out?
questions.explanation: Noor asked whether the narrator still wants the study room, and the narrator answered about not being president. Noor separates the goal from the title.
options: The narrator did not hear her question.
Wanting the study room is separate from winning.
She wants the study room for herself.
The narrator should run again next year.

questions.stem: Why does Marcus look "surprised, and then relieved"?
questions.explanation: Marcus admits he was going to ask the narrator for help, so the offer surprised him and then took a weight off. Nothing suggests a recount or cancelling the room.
options: He thought the narrator wanted the votes recounted.
He had forgotten that the election had happened.
He did not expect the offer but was glad of the help.
He wanted to cancel the study room idea.

questions.stem: The whispering rule was one "nobody followed but everyone liked." This detail suggests the study room
questions.explanation: The light, joking tone shows students were fond of the room and its rule even when they broke it. The room stayed open through the year.
options: was too noisy to be useful for studying
was closed because of all the noise
had strict rules that students feared
became a friendly place students enjoyed

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the theme of the story?
questions.explanation: The narrator loses but builds the study room anyway and is proudest of that title. Marcus says the narrator's speech was better, yet Marcus won, so the best speech did not win.
options: Losing a title doesn't stop you from making a difference.
Student council elections are usually unfair.
Older siblings should stay out of school matters.
The best speech always wins the election.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: A semicolon can join two complete thoughts on its own. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and a semicolon is not followed by and.
options: I studied for hours, the test was still hard.
I studied for hours; the test was still hard.
I studied for hours the test was still hard.
I studied for hours; and the test was still hard.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph. Which sentence would make the best opening sentence?
questions.explanation: The paragraph lists daily care, walks in all weather and costs, which together show how much work a pet is. The other choices match only one detail.
questions.passage: (Opening sentence goes here.) A pet needs food, water and a clean place to sleep every day. Dogs also need walks in every kind of weather, including January. Vet visits and supplies can cost hundreds of dollars a year.
options: Dogs are the most popular pets in many Canadian homes.
Owning a pet takes more work than many people expect.
Vet visits and pet supplies can be very expensive.
Walking a dog in January can be a very cold job.

questions.stem:
Choose the best word or phrase for each blank.

I wanted to join the cross-country team. [[1]], I started running three mornings a week. [[2]], I could run five kilometres without stopping.
questions.explanation: Running more was a result of wanting to join, so So fits. The last sentence tells what happened later, so a time phrase like By October fits.

questions.stem:
Which is the best way to fix this sentence?

The rink was closed, we went sledding instead.
questions.explanation: Adding so after the comma joins the two complete thoughts correctly. Removing the comma makes a run-on, and the extra commas leave the splice in place.
options: The rink was closed we went sledding instead.
The rink, was closed, we went sledding instead.
The rink was closed, so we went sledding instead.
The rink was closed, we, went sledding instead.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph. Which sentence would make the best opening sentence?
questions.explanation: Each detail is a skill or benefit a job gives: managing time, budgeting and building references. The other sentences do not cover those details.
questions.passage: (Opening sentence goes here.) A job teaches teens how to manage their time between school and work. It also gives them their own money and a chance to learn how to budget. Many teens meet new people and build references for future jobs.
options: Teens should save all of the money they earn.
Many employers hire teens in the summer.
A part-time job can teach teens useful skills.
Some teens work in stores and restaurants.

questions.stem: Which sentence is a run-on?
questions.explanation: "My phone died" and "I couldn't call home" are two complete thoughts with nothing joining them. The other sentences use so, a period or because.
options: My phone died, so I couldn't call home.
My phone died. I couldn't call home.
Because my phone died, I couldn't call home.
My phone died I couldn't call home.

questions.stem: Put the sentences in the best order to make a paragraph.
questions.explanation: The time words (when she first moved, the first week, there, by the end of the month) show the order. "There" must come right after the club is named.
options: By the end of the month, the three of them sat together every day.
When Mila first moved to Sudbury, she did not know anyone at school.
There, she met two students who also loved fantasy novels.
During the first week, she joined the reading club at lunch.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The box of old photographs [[1]] in the basement.
questions.explanation: The subject is box (one box), so the verb is is. Photographs is part of the phrase "of old photographs."

questions.stem: Select the sentence that does not belong in this paragraph.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about what national parks do. A favourite hiking snack is a personal detail that does not support that idea.
questions.passage: {{Canada's national parks protect some of the country's most important natural areas.}} {{They give wildlife space to live away from roads and buildings.}} {{They also let visitors hike, camp and paddle in wild places.}} {{My favourite snack on a hike is trail mix.}} {{Park staff study and care for these areas all year.}}

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The players on the senior team [[1]] every morning before school.
questions.explanation: The subject is players, which is plural, so the verb is train. Team is part of the phrase "on the senior team."

questions.stem: Read the paragraph. Which sentence would best conclude it?
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that old electronics do not belong in the garbage, so the best ending tells the reader what to do instead. The others drift to new topics.
questions.passage: Old phones and laptops should never go in the garbage. They contain metals that can leak into soil and water. Many of those metals can also be recovered and used again. Most towns have drop-off depots for electronics. (Concluding sentence goes here.)
options: Laptops usually cost much more than phones do.
When a device dies, take it to a depot.
Some phones keep working for many years.
People have mined metals for thousands of years.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph. Which sentence does not support the main idea?
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about reusable bottles cutting waste. A preference for sparkling water has nothing to do with waste.
questions.passage: (1) Bringing a reusable water bottle to school is an easy way to cut waste. (2) A single bottle can replace hundreds of plastic ones each year. (3) Most schools have fountains or filling stations. (4) Some people prefer sparkling water to plain water.
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by and are plural, so the verb is live (or have lived, are living).
options: My aunt and uncle lives in Thunder Bay.
My aunt and uncle is living in Thunder Bay.
My aunt and uncle live in Thunder Bay.
My aunt and uncle has lived in Thunder Bay.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?
questions.explanation: The bike belongs to the sister, so sister's needs an apostrophe. A plain plural such as bikes never takes one.
options: My sisters bike is in the garage.
My sister's bike's are in the garage.
My sisters' bike's are in the garage.
My sister's bike is in the garage.

questions.stem: A student argues that teens should learn to cook before they finish high school. Which sentence best supports this opinion?
questions.explanation: Saving money is a reason the skill is worth learning. The other sentences are true of some people but give no reason teens should learn to cook.
options: Many restaurants hire teens to wash dishes.
Cooking at home costs much less than eating out.
Some families eat dinner together every night.
Cooking shows are popular with teenagers.

questions.stem:
Read the paragraph. Where should this sentence be added?

"The winning sculpture was a three-metre-tall moose."
questions.explanation: The sentence is about the snow sculptures, so it belongs right after sentence 2, which describes building them.
questions.passage: (1) Our school held its first winter carnival last week. (2) In the morning, students built snow sculptures on the field. (3) After lunch, teams competed in a tug-of-war on the ice. (4) The day ended with hot chocolate in the gym.
options: After sentence 1
After sentence 2
After sentence 3
After sentence 4

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

[[1]] science project won first prize at the fair.
questions.explanation: The project belongs to Jessica, so add an apostrophe and s: Jessica's.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
questions.explanation: In a contraction the apostrophe replaces the missing letters: can't is "cannot." Stops is a verb, so it takes no apostrophe.
options: We cant' leave until the rain stops.
We can't leave until the rain stops.
We ca'nt leave until the rain stops.
We can't leave until the rain stop's.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports the claim that the school's new recycling program is working?
questions.explanation: Evidence that a program works is a result, and cutting garbage in half is a result. The colours, the vote and the history describe the program but not its success.
options: The new bins are blue, green and grey and have labels.
Students voted on where the new bins should be placed.
The school now sends half as much garbage to the landfill.
Recycling programs began in Canada decades ago.

questions.stem:
Choose the best word or phrase for the blank.

Snowshoes spread your weight over a larger area. [[1]], you sink less into deep snow.
questions.explanation: Sinking less is the effect of spreading your weight, so As a result fits. However would signal a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for each blank.

The school changed [[1]] bus schedule, and now [[2]] easier to get home.
questions.explanation: Its shows ownership (the school's schedule). It's means "it is": now it is easier.

questions.stem: A writer wants to end an opinion essay by restating the main opinion. Which sentence does this best?
questions.explanation: "For all these reasons" signals a conclusion, and the sentence restates the opinion. "Another reason" introduces a new point instead of ending.
options: Some students would rather eat lunch with friends in the cafeteria.
Another reason is that the library has computers students can use.
The library was built when the school first opened its doors in 1972.
For all these reasons, our library should stay open at lunch.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: It's is short for "it has" here (it has rained). Its shows that the banks belong to the creek.
options: Its rained all week, and the creek has overflowed it's banks.
It's rained all week, and the creek has overflowed it's banks.
Its rained all week, and the creek has overflowed its banks.
It's rained all week, and the creek has overflowed its banks.

questions.stem:
Choose the best word or phrase for the blank.

Some plants need full sun. [[1]], ferns grow best in the shade.
questions.explanation: Ferns are the opposite case, so a contrast phrase fits. For example would wrongly make ferns an example of sun-loving plants.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for each blank.

[[1]] going to leave [[2]] bikes over [[3]] by the fence.
questions.explanation: They're means "they are," their shows the bikes belong to them, and there points to a place.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives an example to support the idea that small acts of kindness matter?
questions.explanation: An example is a specific case, and the shared notes are a real act of kindness with a clear result. The other sentences are general statements.
options: When a classmate shared notes after I was sick, I caught up in a day.
Kindness is something that every community needs in order to thrive.
Some people seem to find it easier to be kind than others do.
Being kind usually takes less effort than being mean to someone.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for each blank.

My brother is taller [[1]] me, but I can run faster [[2]] he can.
questions.explanation: Both blanks compare two people, so both take than. Then is about time.

questions.stem:
Choose the best word or phrase for the blank.

There are many ways to save energy at home. [[1]], you can turn off the lights when you leave a room.
questions.explanation: Turning off lights is one of the many ways, so For example introduces it. However, Instead and In contrast all signal a contrast.

questions.stem: A student argues that winter break should be longer. Which sentence best answers someone who disagrees?
questions.explanation: Answering the other side means naming its concern (a later end to the year) and responding to it. The other sentences ignore what an opponent would say.
options: Winter break is the best part of the whole school year.
A later end in June is worth it if students come back rested.
Many families like to travel during the winter break.
Some schools also give students a week off in March.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for each blank.

We had [[1]] snow days this year [[2]] last year.
questions.explanation: Snow days can be counted, so fewer is correct; less is for amounts. Than makes the comparison.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses accept or except correctly?
questions.explanation: Except means "leaving out," so everyone except Lena is right. To accept is to receive, which the last two sentences need.
options: Everyone accept Lena finished early.
I will except your kind invitation.
Please except my apology for being late.
Everyone except Lena finished early.

questions.stem: Which sentence would make the best main opinion (thesis) for an opinion essay?
questions.explanation: A thesis states a clear opinion the essay can support. The others are a fact, a personal detail and a question.
options: First aid courses are offered by many groups.
I took a first aid course last summer.
Every Grade 9 student should take a first aid course.
What is first aid, and who teaches it?

questions.stem: Put the steps in the best order for instructions on making a jar terrarium.
questions.explanation: First, Next, Then and Finally give the order, and it makes sense too: clean the jar, plant, water, then close it.
options: Then water the plants lightly.
Finally, put the lid on and set the jar near a window.
First, rinse the jar and remove the label.
Next, fill it with soil and a few small plants.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

The coach gave the trophy to Ravi and [[1]].
questions.explanation: After to, use me. Test it by removing Ravi: "gave the trophy to me," not "to I."

questions.stem: A student's paragraph says that walking to school is good for students. Which sentence would be the best addition?
questions.explanation: Exercise is a benefit of walking, which supports the paragraph. Living too far away is a point against it, and the last two are off topic.
options: Some students live too far away to walk to school.
My little brother takes the bus to his school.
School buses are yellow so drivers can see them.
A twenty-minute walk gives students exercise before class.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: The pronouns are doing the action, so use she and I. Test each alone: "she is working," "I am working."
options: Her and me are working on the project.
She and I are working on the project.
Me and her are working on the project.
Her and I are working on the project.

questions.stem: An essay's first body paragraph is about the benefits of school uniforms. Which sentence would best begin a new paragraph about their drawbacks?
questions.explanation: However signals the turn from benefits to drawbacks and names the new topic. Saving time is another benefit, and "In conclusion" ends the essay.
options: Uniforms save families time every morning.
Many schools in Ontario have uniforms.
In conclusion, uniforms are a good idea.
However, uniforms also have some downsides.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

To [[1]] should I give the permission form?
questions.explanation: After the preposition to, use whom. Who's means "who is," and whose shows ownership.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph. Which sentence should be removed?
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains why swimming is an important safety skill. A favourite pool's water slide is off topic.
questions.passage: (1) Learning to swim is an important safety skill. (2) My favourite pool has a twisty water slide. (3) Canada has thousands of lakes and rivers, and many families spend summers near water. (4) Knowing how to swim can stop a dangerous situation from becoming deadly.
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4

questions.stem: Which sentence keeps the verb tense consistent?
questions.explanation: All three actions happened in the past, so every verb is past tense: reached, set up, went.
options: We reached the lake, set up the tent and go for a swim.
We reach the lake, set up the tent and went for a swim.
We reached the lake, sets up the tent and went for a swim.
We reached the lake, set up the tent and went for a swim.

questions.stem:
Read the paragraph. Where should this sentence be added?

"Even our dog would not eat it."
questions.explanation: The sentence is about the ruined loaf, so it belongs right after sentence 3, which describes the loaf coming out flat and hard.
questions.passage: (1) My first try at baking bread was a disaster. (2) I forgot the yeast, so the dough never rose. (3) The loaf came out flat and hard as a brick. (4) The next weekend, I tried again and followed every step.
options: After sentence 1
After sentence 2
After sentence 3
After sentence 4

questions.stem: Which title best fits a report about how beavers build dams and change the land around them?
questions.explanation: The report covers dam building and its effect on the land, and only the first title names both. The others are about money, protecting trees or winter.
options: Why You Will Find a Beaver on the Nickel
Beavers: Builders That Change the Land
How to Keep Beavers Away from Your Trees
Where Beavers Go When Winter Comes

questions.stem:
Choose the correct word for the blank.

By the time we got to the theatre, the movie [[1]] already started.
questions.explanation: The movie started before another past event (we got there), so use had started.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: With have, use the form seen. Saw stands alone ("I saw it"), and seen always needs a helper such as have.
options: I have saw that movie twice.
I have seen that movie twice.
I seen that movie twice.
I have seed that movie twice.

questions.stem: A student is writing that the town should keep its free outdoor rink open longer each night. Which TWO sentences best support this opinion? Choose two.
questions.explanation: A rink that is still busy at closing time and families who depend on it are both reasons to stay open longer. The others do not give a reason for longer hours.
options: Some people prefer swimming to skating.
The rink is busy every evening right up until it closes.
Families who cannot afford arena fees use the free rink.
The arena downtown has a snack bar.
Outdoor rinks need cold weather to stay frozen.

questions.stem: Which sentence would make the best first sentence of an essay arguing that teenagers should learn first aid?
questions.explanation: A good opening hooks the reader and leads toward the opinion. "In conclusion" and "Next" belong later in an essay, and kit sizes are off topic.
options: First aid kits come in many sizes and colours.
Anyone could be the first person to reach an emergency.
In conclusion, first aid is a skill that saves lives.
Next, this essay will discuss how to do CPR.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
questions.explanation: Put the comma after the whole opening clause, "When the bell rang." The other commas split a subject from its verb.
options: When the bell rang the students, grabbed their coats.
When, the bell rang, the students grabbed their coats.
When the bell rang, the students grabbed their coats.
When the bell, rang the students grabbed their coats.

questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: Amara is the subject of both verbs (finished, went), so no comma is needed. A comma never separates a subject from its verb.
options: Amara, finished her homework and went to bed.
Amara finished, her homework and went to bed.
Amara finished her homework and, went to bed.
Amara finished her homework and went to bed.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that does not belong in this paragraph.
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about what the class learned at the science centre. The bus driver's name has nothing to do with that.
questions.passage: {{Our class trip to the science centre taught us a lot.}} {{We tried experiments with electricity and magnets.}} {{The bus driver's name was Mr. Kowalski.}} {{A guide showed us how engineers test bridges.}} {{By the end, many of us wanted to learn more about engineering.}}

questions.stem: Put the sentences in the best order to make a paragraph.
questions.explanation: The paragraph follows the geese in time: they leave, stop along the way, arrive and nest, then the goslings hatch.
options: Along the way, they stop at lakes and fields to rest and eat.
Every spring, Canada geese fly north to nest.
A few weeks later, fuzzy goslings hatch.
When they reach their nesting grounds, each pair builds a nest near water.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
questions.explanation: A comma follows the opener "For the trip" and separates the items in the list. No comma goes between bring and what is brought.
options: For the trip, bring a sleeping bag, a flashlight and warm socks.
For the trip bring, a sleeping bag a flashlight and warm socks.
For the trip, bring a sleeping bag a flashlight, and warm socks.
For the trip, bring, a sleeping bag, a flashlight and warm socks.

questions.stem: A student writes: "Our school should offer a cooking class." Which sentence best explains why?
questions.explanation: A reason explains why the class matters, and needing to feed yourself soon does that. The others describe classes, rooms or the writer's hobby.
options: Many students will soon live on their own and need to feed themselves.
Cooking classes are already taught in some high schools in Ontario.
A cooking class would make use of the kitchen near the cafeteria.
I really like to cook pasta with my older brother on weekends.

questions.stem:
Select the word that is spelled incorrectly.

{{Because}} of the {{weather}}, the {{tournament}} was {{definately}} {{cancelled}}.
questions.explanation: Definitely is spelled d-e-f-i-n-i-t-e-l-y; it contains the word finite. Cancelled with two l's is the usual Canadian spelling.

questions.stem:
Choose the best word or phrase for each blank.

Biking to school is good exercise. [[1]], it saves money on bus fare. [[2]], some students worry about riding in winter.
questions.explanation: Saving money is a second benefit, so In addition fits. Worrying about winter is a drawback, so However signals the contrast.

questions.stem:
Select the word that is spelled incorrectly.

It was {{embarassing}} when my {{neighbour}} saw me {{practising}} my {{speech}} in the {{backyard}}.
questions.explanation: Embarrassing has a double r and a double s. Neighbour and practising (the verb) are the Canadian spellings.

questions.stem: Read the paragraph. Which sentence best states its main idea?
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives benefits for students (fresher food that tastes better) and for farmers (steady sales). The apple detail is one example, not the main idea.
questions.passage: Our school cafeteria now buys apples, potatoes and carrots from farms less than 100 kilometres away. The food is fresher because it spends less time on trucks. Local farmers earn steady money from a buyer they can count on. And students say the apples taste better than the ones the cafeteria used to serve.
options: Apples are the most popular food in the school cafeteria.
Buying food from nearby farms helps both students and farmers.
Trucks carry food long distances across the country.
Farmers need more customers to stay in business.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Necessary has one c and a double s: n-e-c-e-s-s-a-r-y. A memory trick is "one collar, two sleeves."
options: neccessary
necessery
neccesary
necessary

questions.stem: Which change would best improve the organization of this paragraph?
questions.explanation: Sentence 1 begins with Finally, so it should come last, after First and Next. Then the trip is told in order.
questions.passage: (1) Finally, we put up our tent beside the lake. (2) First, we packed the canoe. (3) Next, we paddled across the bay.
options: Move sentence 1 to the end.
Move sentence 3 to the start.
Remove sentence 2.
Join sentences 2 and 3.

questions.stem: Which sentence would best support the opinion that public libraries are still important?
questions.explanation: People relying on libraries for job applications shows they still matter today. A long history or opening hours do not show present importance.
options: Libraries have existed for thousands of years.
Some people prefer to buy books, not borrow them.
Many people use library computers to apply for jobs.
Many libraries are open on Saturday mornings.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
questions.explanation: Months and the full names of places, such as Lake Superior, take capitals, as does the first word of a sentence. Family is a common noun.
options: In July, my family drove to Lake Superior.
In july, my family drove to lake Superior.
In July, my Family drove to Lake superior.
in July, my family drove to Lake Superior.
